segments.title: The morning you knew, and the catalyst
sections: The Morning You Already Knew The Direction
Catalysts Set The Clock, Not The Direction

cues.text: You know the morning. CPI, the monthly inflation report, came in below forecast, the overnight session jumped, and a chat room wrote "trend day up".
By 9:47 a.m. you had bought a dip in the middle of the range. At 10:05 you sold a push because the RSI, a momentum reading, was high.
Both stopped out. Neither came from a level, a price marked before the session.
Each input was used for the wrong job. Four opinions, zero prices. Nobody asked the chart.
Now, the idea. Every trade here traces one chain: idea, setup, trigger, construction.
A setup is a location and a read together. A trigger is the price event that puts you in. Construction is the stop, the size and the entry.
The idea comes first, finished before the session opens.
Now, catalysts. A catalyst is an event that brings participants at a known or sudden time: a Tier One release, one you go flat for, like CPI, a Fed decision, a headline.
It sets the clock. It can print a level. It never sets a direction.
The example. At 8:30 a.m. CPI prints below forecast. At 8:31 the MNQ, the micro Nasdaq future, trades 50 points higher and prints the overnight high. By 9:05 it has given most of it back.
The release came at a known time, brought a burst of activity, and printed a level. It did not tell you a direction.
Neither does a macro theme, or yields, the dollar, oil or the other index.
The rule: a catalyst goes on the sheet, your written pre-market plan, as an event, a time and any level it printed. The surprise is never written.
For a Tier One release, add T minus 5 and T plus 2: flat five minutes before, no new entries until two minutes after.
The figure behind that rule. TradingStats app data, June 2020 to May 2026, across 72 non-farm payroll releases.
The surprise matched the direction of NQ, the full-size Nasdaq future, in 33 of the 70 scored. That is n equals 70.
About a coin flip. Knowing which way the number surprised did not tell you which way price went.
Getting it wrong is "CPI cool, longs only", or a short at 8:33 because the number was hot.
It reveals a number someone else published choosing your side before any level was tested. The fix: strike any word about the number, hot, cool, beat or miss, before 9:25.

segments.title: The calendar, and the room
sections: The Calendar Sets Activity, Not Price
ATR Sets The Room; RSI Sets Nothing

cues.text: Some sessions differ for reasons printed on a calendar months ahead. Forced orders, the ones that must be placed whatever the price, bunch into known windows: context about activity.
One: OpEx, options expiration, the monthly expiry of listed index options.
Two: quad witching, the quarterly expiry Friday, when index futures expire the same day as options.
Three: turn of month, the last sessions of one month and the first of the next, when rebalancing is scheduled.
The calendar line is nouns and dates: turn of month, month-end close is the next session, not expiry week, not roll week, the week the contract rolls, Tier One CPI at 8:30 a.m.
It changes your expectation of activity, never which side a branch, one if-then line of your plan, takes. The calendar is a timetable. It is not a prophecy.
The rule: calendar items are nouns on the calendar line. They set expectations of activity, never a direction.
Getting it wrong is "OpEx Friday, it will pin, fade every move". It reveals a timetable turned into a forecast.
The fix: any up, down, long, short or should is struck through. Copy the nouns into each trade’s journal notes, so your record shows whether those days differ.
Now, ATR, average true range: the average of a bar’s full travel over a set number of bars, commonly 14. It says how far price usually goes, never where.
The example. The 14-day ATR is 310 points. The overnight range runs 21,880 to 22,010.
From the overnight low, an ordinary session reaches about 22,190. From the overnight high, about 21,700. Those two prices are the room frame.
A target, the price a trade aims at, beyond the frame asks for an unusual session. ATR sets the room for targets, never the stop, the order that takes you out when wrong.
Now, RSI, the relative strength index: 0 to 100 for how one-sided the last 14 sessions were. Say it reads 74. That describes the past, not whether the move is spent.
RSI at 74 is a report. It is not a forecast. So it has no slot on the sheet.
The rule: ATR goes on the sheet as one number in points and the two frame prices. No other indicator reading goes on the sheet.
Getting it wrong is “RSI 74, overbought, look for shorts”. It reveals the past read as a forecast. The fix: one indicator line; a target outside the frame is marked outside room.

check.why: 21,880 plus 310 is 22,190. 22,010 minus 310 is 21,700. An ordinary session's travel from each end.

check.q: A sheet says "RSI 74, overbought, look for shorts". What does it reveal?
options: A description of the past read as a forecast
A calendar noun turned into a direction
check.why: RSI describes how one-sided the recent run was. It is never a thesis, a trigger, an exit or a direction.

cues.text: Now the inputs become an idea. An idea is a conditional statement written before the session, made of branches. A branch is one conditional line of the plan.
One: the thesis, the if-then part. A named level, written as a zone, a band with a near edge and a far edge, the trigger that must fire there, and the level it targets.
Two: the invalidation, the price at which the thesis is wrong, judged on a candle close of a stated timeframe.
It sits at or behind the zone’s far edge. Written before the session, never moved during it.
Three: conviction, a label of strong, moderate or thin for how much structure stands behind the branch.
The inputs from the last two segments enter a branch in exactly three places.
One: context and the catalyst decide which levels are worth a branch at all.
Two: the room frame decides whether the target is reachable on an ordinary session.
Three: the clock decides whether a Tier One release lands inside your window, 9:30 to 11 a.m.
Conviction is counted, not felt. Your gut does not get a point. Three checks, one point each.
Zone: the zone holds more than one level from your list, like the prior-day high and the overnight high within a few points of each other.
Path: no other level from your list sits between the zone and the target.
Room and clock: the target sits inside the room frame, and no Tier One release falls inside the window.
Three points is strong. Two is moderate. One or none is thin. The reason names the check that failed: "moderate, prior-day low in the path". Conviction never touches size.
The rule: every idea is a thesis at a named zone, an invalidation price with its candle timeframe, and a conviction counted from the three checks with a one-clause reason.
An idea without an invalidation is No Setup, the tag for a trade taken on feel.
Getting it wrong is "looking for longs above the prior high, feels strong".
It reveals inputs turned into a mood, so there is no price at which the idea ends.
The fix: write each branch backwards. Invalidation first.
Then zone and trigger.
Then target, then the three checks, and the label last.

segments.title: Two reads, and whose read it is
sections: Two Reads: The Market And Your Execution

cues.text: An idea can be right and the trade still lose. A trade can win off an idea that was wrong. One result grading both teaches you neither.
One: the market read, your judgment before the session of where business can happen: which levels get branches, the room, the clock.
Afterwards, one question: did price do at the level what a branch said, or did the nothing case, the no-trade line, hold?
Two: the execution read, how you acted: did the trigger fire before entry, the stop sit behind structure, size and exit follow the plan?
Graded by the grade, A-plus to C, and the execution mark, pass or fail on whether the exit followed the plan. Never by the result.
A hypothetical illustration, not a trade record. The branch: accept above the prior-day high zone, a 5-minute close beyond it within 15 minutes of the first touch.
A Pause N Go, Module 13’s trigger, fires on the pullback; target the prior-week high. Price accepted, paused and went.
You entered early, before the pause resolved, and the first wobble stopped you out. Market read: right. Execution read: no trigger yet, entry marked down.
The rule: grade the market read and the execution read on separate lines, neither by the trade’s result. A mid-range win says nothing good about either.
Getting it wrong is rewriting your idea process after a losing day when every branch played out as written, or keeping a habit because it won.
It reveals the result grading everything. The fix: write both lines before you look at the day's R, your result in units of risk.
Now, whose read it is. A desk’s note, a chat’s “trend day up”, a feed of confident calls. The pull is strongest when your sheet looks uncertain.
A borrowed call names no level and no trigger.
No invalidation, no conviction you can count. No price can prove “trend day up” wrong. Confidence is free. The trade it talks you into is not.
The rule: another trader’s call is a label, not an input. Rebuild it as your own branch, zone, trigger and invalidation price, or it is off the sheet.
Borrowing a branch is opening the chat before the sheet, or moving a branch from thin to strong because a respected account agreed. Conviction gone social.
The fix: the sheet comes first. Chats, feeds and notes stay closed until 9:25.
And a reason naming a person or a post is struck through.

check.q: Your branch's level held exactly as written, but you entered before the trigger fired and stopped out. Which read was wrong?
options: The execution read; the market read was right
The market read; the execution was fine
check.why: The branch played out, so the market read was right. The early entry is an execution leak.

check.q: A trade from the middle of the range happens to win. What does the win say?
options: Nothing good about either: the plan never made that read and there was no level
check.why: A result does not grade a read. The plan never named that place.

check.q: When do you write the two read lines in the evening review?
options: After you see the day's R
Before you look at the day's R
check.why: Read lines first, then the R, so the result does not grade everything.

check.q: A respected account in a chat posts the same call as your branch. What happens to your conviction?
options: It is counted from the three checks only; a reason naming a person is struck through
The account goes in the reason clause
check.why: Conviction comes only from the three checks. It is not social.

cues.text: A hypothetical illustration, not a trade record: a composite MNQ morning, invented prices. It stops at 9:25 a.m., before the open.
Catalyst: CPI at 8:30 a.m., already past. It printed the overnight high, 22,010, at 8:31. Beat or miss is not on the sheet.
Calendar line: turn of month, month-end close is the next session, not expiry week, not roll week.
Room: ATR 310, frame 21,700 to 22,190. Struck from the sheet: RSI 74, which has no slot, and the chat’s “trend day up”, which has no price.
Context at 9:05 a.m. Price is 21,968, inside the prior-day range, 21,840 to 21,995, and above prior-day value, the band where most of the volume traded.
Seven zones from your list, all inside the room frame, so the frame removes none.
The two zones that each hold two levels are the edges of the range the release printed. They get branches.
The value area high, the top of that band, and the point of control, the single price with the most volume, go to the nothing case.

Branch one, written backwards. Invalidation: a 5-minute close back below 21,989. Thesis: accept above 22,010 within 15 minutes of the first touch, a Pause N Go fires on the pullback, target the prior-week high, 22,120.
Checks: zone, two levels, yes. Path, nothing between, yes. Room and clock, yes. Strong, three of three.

Branch two. Invalidation: a 5-minute close back above 21,886. Thesis: accept below 21,879, a Pause N Go on the pullback, target the low-volume node, a price where little traded, on the higher timeframe, 21,786.
Checks: zone, yes. Path, the prior-day low zone sits between, no. Room and clock, yes. Moderate: prior-day low in the path.
The nothing case: between 21,886 and 21,989 without acceptance outside it, no trade. A gap open, above 21,995 or below 21,840: no gap branch, so no trade.
Notice what the inputs did. The release gave a time and a level.
The calendar, a noun.
ATR, two prices that checked the targets.
None picked a side. The widest line on the sheet still says no trade.
The rule: the inputs choose the levels, the room and the clock. Only the levels choose the branches. Stop, size and entry come later, at the trigger, from Module 14.
Getting it wrong here was opening the chat at 8:50 a.m., before the sheet. It reveals the borrowed label arriving first. The fix is the order: sheet first, chat closed.

cues.text: Take your last five pre-market sheets, Module 16’s morning plan. Score each one a point per line that is true. Seven lines.
One, catalyst: event, time, T minus 5 and T plus 2, and no word about the number.
Two, calendar: nouns and dates only.
Three, room: ATR in points and the two frame prices, no other indicator value.
Four, thesis: every branch names a zone, a behaviour, a trigger and a target.
Five, invalidation: every branch has a price and its candle timeframe.
Six, conviction: strong, moderate or thin, counted from the three checks, with a reason.
Seven, your own: nothing from another trader's view anywhere on the sheet.
Now, reading it. Seven of seven is an idea. Six of seven is a mood with a time stamp.
If any sheet missed line five, trades taken from it were No Setup, and the invalidation line is the first fix.
If line seven failed on any of the five, write your next five sheets with every chat, feed and note closed until 9:25.
If two or more sheets scored under seven for another reason, fix the line you miss most often first.
Getting it wrong is scoring from memory and giving every line a yes. It reveals the sheet you remember, not the one you wrote.
The assignment. Before you open anyone else’s view, write one line: the catalysts with their times, the calendar line in nouns, and ATR in points with the frame, low to high. That is all.
In one line: an idea is your levels, your room and your clock turned into branches a price can prove wrong. No input, and no one else's call, decides the direction.
Where it goes next. Module 16, the pre-market routine, writes this idea on the sheet each morning, finished by 9:25. Module 15, writing the plan, turns ideas into a full plan.
Modules 10 and 11 teach acceptance and rejection at the level. Module 13 covers the Pause N Go, and Module 14 turns a branch into a stop, a size and an entry.
Module 18 grades the two reads in the evening review. The forced flow behind the calendar is in Module 4.
Sources: TradingStats NFP data on NQ, June 2020 to May 2026, and the Cboe SPX options specifications.

check.q: A sheet scores six of seven because line five failed. What are the trades taken from it?
check.why: A branch with no invalidation is No Setup, and the invalidation line is the first thing to fix.

check.q: Line seven failed on one of your five sheets. What do the next five do?
options: Get written with every chat, feed and note closed until 9:25 a.m.
check.why: The sheet is written before any outside view is opened.

check.q: What is the one-line assignment?
options: The catalysts with times, the calendar line in nouns, and ATR with the frame
A list of every indicator reading
The chat's view of the day
check.why: Catalysts and times, calendar nouns, and ATR in points with the frame, low to high. One line.

check.q: You score your last five sheets from memory. What does it reveal?
options: You are scoring the sheet you remember, not the one you wrote
check.why: Score only what is on the paper.

questions.q: Which input sets the clock but never the direction?
questions.why: A catalyst brings activity at a known or sudden time and can print a level. It never picks a side.

questions.q: ATR is 310 and the overnight range is 21,880 to 22,010, so the frame is 21,700 to 22,190. A target at 22,300 is…
options: Inside the frame, so it stands
Allowed if the catalyst is Tier One
Outside the frame: marked outside room
questions.why: A target beyond the frame asks for an unusual session. It is marked outside room.

questions.q: Which of these is an idea?
options: If price accepts above the prior-day high zone and a Pause N Go fires, target the prior-week high; wrong on a 5-minute close back below the zone; moderate, prior-day low in the path
questions.why: A thesis at a named zone, an invalidation with its timeframe, and a counted conviction with a reason.

questions.q: Where do the inputs enter a branch?
options: Three places: which levels get a branch, whether the target is reachable, whether a Tier One lands in the window
questions.why: Context and catalyst, the room frame, and the clock. Nothing else.

questions.q: How are the market read and the execution read graded?
options: By the result of each trade
Separately, and neither by the trade's result
questions.why: Two lines, written before you look at the day's R.

questions.q: Which of these is not one of the three conviction checks?
options: The direction of the CPI surprise
Path: nothing between zone and target
questions.why: The surprise is never written on the sheet and never counts.

questions.q: TradingStats app data, NFP releases on NQ, June 2020 to May 2026 (72 releases, n=70 scored): how often did the direction of the surprise match the direction of price?
questions.why: About a coin flip. Knowing which way the number surprised did not tell you which way price went.

options: A label, not an input, unless you rebuild it as your own branch
questions.why: If it cannot be rebuilt with a zone, a trigger and an invalidation price, it is not on the sheet.
